# What the man at the large machine does

**Short answer: he works the machine's controls for that table — he presses/turns the round, plate‑shaped selector dial on the console (the dials are labelled with the courses, e.g. "PLATES", "DUCK SOUP", "OYSTER…") and then grasps and pulls the big hand lever beside it. Throwing that lever sends the order down the pipework, and the jointed, white‑gloved pincer claw on the end of the pipe over the diners' table swings down and gathers up the two men's spoons and plates.**

## The setting

The film is the French release ("INVENTION MODERNE") of a Charley Bowers automatic‑restaurant comedy, in which the inventor (called "Bricolo" in the French titles) demonstrates a fully mechanised restaurant to his boss. The dining room is served not by waiters but by machinery: telescoping rods with white‑gloved mechanical hands and pincer claws come out of numbered hatches in the service wall and down out of the pipes that run above the tables. Two elderly gentlemen in the dining room (their table cards read "4" and "6") order oyster soup ("Une soupe aux huîtres pour deux") and are served, and cleared, entirely by these mechanical hands.

## The large machine

The "large machine" is the giant control console at the back of the restaurant. It is marked "TABLES" on a signboard across the top; below that are rows of round, dish‑like dials, each engraved with the name of a dish or item of service ("PLATES", "DUCK SOUP", "OYSTER…"); there is a large upright hand lever set among the dials; and there are flywheels and pipework below, with "GARBAGE" stencilled on the lower part of the housing. The man operating it stands at the console in shirtsleeves with a headset on, so he can hear the orders and set the machine for each table in turn; his boss, in overcoat and bowler hat, watches over his shoulder.

## The specific action that triggers the claw

The film makes the cause and effect explicit by cutting straight from the operator's hands on the console to the result at the table. Two control movements are shown in close‑up:

1. **He presses/turns the round dish dial.** At roughly 9 min 34 s (~974.5 s) the film cuts to a giant close‑up of his hand coming down on the round dial engraved "PLATES" (with "OYSTER…" on the dial below it) and pressing/rotating it. He is selecting which service is wanted. Immediately after this the mechanical service arrives at the two gentlemen's table.

2. **He pulls the big hand lever.** At roughly 17 min 56 s (~1075.7–1076.8 s) there is an extreme close‑up of his arm reaching into frame, taking hold of the machine's large hand lever (the one standing next to the "DUCK SOUP" dial, under the "TABLES" sign) and hauling it over. The film cuts directly from that lever pull to the two men's table, where the arm on the pipe does its work. The same lever throw is used earlier (~890.5 s) to launch the flying tablecloth and table setting, which establishes for the audience that pulling this lever is what makes the machinery act on a table.

So the answer to "what does he do" is: **he selects the table's service on the console — pushing/turning the labelled round dial (the plate/dish selector, the one marked "PLATES") — and then throws the machine's big hand lever.** That single lever pull is the trigger. The motion runs through the flywheels and the pipes, the pipe above the diners' table discharges its telescoping rod, and the pincer claw on the end of it reaches down over the table, closes on the men's used spoons and plates and carries them off — the dishes go away up the pipe to the "GARBAGE"/washing side of the machine, leaving the two men sitting at an empty table, staring, with their food snatched from under them.

## Why this reading is well supported

- The console is the only machine in the film with human controls, and the operator is the only man shown touching them.
- Every time the film wants us to understand that the machinery has been set in motion, it cuts from a close‑up of his hand on a control (dial or lever) to the table or hatch where the mechanical arm then acts — the tablecloth gag at ~890 s, the plate delivery after the "PLATES" dial at ~974.5 s, and the table shot immediately after the lever pull at ~1076 s.
- The dials are labelled with dishes and services, i.e. they are the "order" selectors; the big lever is the "go" control that actually dispatches the mechanical arm down the pipe.

criteria.justification: The candidate explicitly states he throws the machine's big hand lever and that "That single lever pull is the trigger" causing the pincer claw to collect the men's spoons and plates.

# Answer

**What the man does:** the operator of the big kitchen machine (the young inventor in shirt‑sleeves wearing headphones, standing at the control console while the restaurant boss in a bowler hat watches) reaches across the console and **pulls a lever**. The close‑up of his hand shows the sequence: his hand first presses one of the round dish buttons on the console (the row marked "DUCK SOUP", "OYSTERS", etc.), then slides over to the tall upright lever standing next to those buttons, grips its top, pulls it across from the button side over to the other side (next to the bell‑shaped weight hanging beside it), holds it there for a moment, and then lets go of it.

**What that causes:** the pipe hanging over table 4 (the big bell‑mouthed funnel that looks like a lamp shade above the two elderly diners) drops a mechanical white‑gloved pincer/claw on an arm out of its mouth. The claw comes down onto the table, grabs the right‑hand diner's soup plate together with his spoon and lifts them straight up into the pipe; then it comes down a second time and takes the left‑hand diner's soup plate and spoon as well, clearing the table while the two men are still in the middle of eating. The diners throw up their hands and stare up at the pipe in astonishment.

**Where in the clip:** machine‑room shot ≈ 1074.4–1075.7 s (operator reaches across the console); close‑up of the hand pressing the button and pulling the lever ≈ 1075.7–1076.8 s; table 4 scene ≈ 1076.8–1085.4 s, with the claw taking the right diner's plate and spoon at ≈ 1082.4–1082.9 s and the left diner's at ≈ 1084.6–1085.4 s.

**In one sentence:** he pulls the lever on the machine's control console (right after pressing a dish button), and that sends the gloved pincer‑claw down out of the funnel‑pipe over the table to snatch away the two diners' plates and spoons.

muse-code+muse-spark-1.3@xhigh.answer:
The film is Charley Bowers' "Invention Moderne." The young man is Bricolo, the inventor, demonstrating his large automatic-restaurant machine to the owner, Monsieur Boufaleuil, the man in the hat and overcoat.

The large machine stands in the kitchen area. It has a slanted panel of round food buttons labeled MASHED POTATOES, BROILER, SPAGHETTI, MILK, HASH and others, two large numbered wheels at the bottom, the word GARBAGE on the side, overhead pipes, and a TABLES indicator. Bricolo wears a telephone headset to take orders from the dining room and works the panel while the owner watches.

The two eaters are the two old men in dark suits seated opposite each other at the white-clothed table under the large funnel-shaped hood, with table numbers 6 on the left and 4 on the right. They are eating soup.

What Bricolo does is pull the large hand lever on the side of the control panel. In close-up his right hand is shown grasping the dark flat pivoted lever beside the round buttons and pulling it from its angled rest position up to vertical, while he continues to work the button panel for the owner.

That lever throw operates the overhead-pipe circuit for those tables. Its effect at the table is that the small two-pronged pincer claw that lives in the centre mouth of the large funnel/pipe above the table comes down into view. It first seizes a spoon and then a plate, lifting each up into the funnel. The film shows the white spoon gripped in the pincer jaws below the hood, then a plate rising and disappearing into the hood, while the two men look up and gesture with their meal interrupted.

criteria.justification: The candidate states he operates a single large hand lever on the control panel, moving it from its angled rest position to vertical, which triggers the pincer claw to take the spoon and plate.
